value.overview: The Black-and-yellow Silky-flycatcher (Phainoptila melanoxantha) is a small, colorful songbird of the high mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is one of the silky-flycatchers, a small Neotropical family related to waxwings. The species is usually found in cool, humid forests, forest edges, and shrublands at middle and high elevations. Its contrasting black, yellow, and white plumage and preference for mountain habitats make it a distinctive bird of Central American highlands.
value.classification: The Black-and-yellow Silky-flycatcher belongs to the family Ptiliogonatidae, the silky-flycatchers. Its scientific name is Phainoptila melanoxantha.
value.identification: This compact silky-flycatcher has strongly contrasting plumage. Adults show a dark head and upperparts, black wings and tail, and bright yellow underparts, with pale or white markings in the wing and tail areas. Females and immature birds are generally duller than adult males. It has a short, broad bill and a fairly long tail. The species is often detected while moving through foliage or visiting fruiting trees, rather than sitting in the open for long periods.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs in the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. In Costa Rica, it is a mainly montane bird found along the Cordillera de Talamanca and other suitable high-elevation ranges, including humid highland forest, mossy forest, forest borders, wooded clearings, and dense mountain shrubland. It commonly occupies elevations from roughly 1,500 to above 3,000 meters, depending on locality. Important habitat includes mature upland forest as well as secondary growth and edge vegetation that produce berries and other small fruits.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident in its mountain range, but it can make local or seasonal movements along elevation gradients in Costa Rica, especially in response to food availability and weather. It is not a long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place during the wetter part of the year, with timing varying by elevation and locality. The species builds a small cup-shaped nest in vegetation, usually in a shrub or low tree, using plant fibers, moss, and other fine materials. Clutches are small, commonly containing about two eggs. Both adults are involved in caring for the young. Details of nesting behavior are less thoroughly documented than for many widespread lowland birds.
value.dietFeeding: The Black-and-yellow Silky-flycatcher feeds mainly on small fruits and berries, including those produced by montane shrubs and trees. It also takes insects and other small arthropods, particularly when feeding young. Birds usually forage in pairs or small groups, moving through foliage and making short flights to seize fruit or prey. Fruiting plants are especially important, and the species may join mixed-species feeding flocks in mountain forests.
value.behavior: This species is active and social, commonly occurring in pairs or small groups and sometimes associating with other highland birds. It moves through dense vegetation with quick hops and short flights, often pausing briefly before continuing to another perch. Its flight is direct but usually limited to short distances within the forest. Vocalizations help reveal its presence, because the bird can remain partly hidden in foliage. It may defend a breeding area while remaining generally unobtrusive.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not precisely quantified. No strong evidence indicates that the species currently meets the criteria for a threatened category, although its restricted mountain range makes monitoring valuable.
